newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen warns of Cambodia crisis if king abdicates.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen warns of Cambodia crisis if king abdicates.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen on Saturday warned of a political crisis and bloodshed if King Norodom Sihanouk abdicated and said the royal family should stay out of politics.

"I strongly urge the king not to abdicate, otherwise people from each party will fight each other," he said in a speech aired on radio, reiterating that local and national polls expected in 1997 and 1998 would have to be scrapped if the king stepped down.

Hun Sen claimed his coalition government partner but political rival, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh of the royalist FUNCINPEC party, had made a speech on March 8 encouraging Sihanouk to abdicate and fight elections.

"Ranariddh supports the king's abdication, I appeal to the king not to abdicate. If he abdicates there will be a throne crisis, a political crisis," said the second prime minister, speaking at a provincial school opening.
Sihanouk, who is in China for a periodic medical checkup and treatment, said last month he had been thinking of abdicating following mounting attacks on himself and the royal family.
But the 74-year-old monarch, who rules but does not govern, pledged he would never take part in the general elections or form a party for the polls.
Ranariddh, speaking after the king's feelings were made public by the palace on February 26, urged his father to stay on the throne as the country's main unifying figure.

The prince and Hun Sen formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993. Relations dived after Ranariddh demanded a fairer share of power in March last year and tensions were exacerbated in recent months as the rivals vied to win the support of thousands of Khmer Rouge guerrilla defectors.
But the two men, who have in recent weeks been forming rival election alliances with other parties, earlier this month pledged to improve their working relations for the sake of the country.
Hun Sen said he supported the monarchy but believed the royal family should stay out of politics, adding this could be enshrined in the constitution or approved by referendum.
He said if members of the royal family wanted to take part in politics they should renounce their titles, adding it was hard to defend royals when they were associated with one political party.
"They can fight us, but when we fight back they take the king to put in front -- this is unjust."
"This is an attack on the institution of the monarchy, on the FUNCINPEC party and on the NUF alliance," said one Cambodian analyst, referring to the royalist-led National United Front.
"This is the road to the election already," he added.
Some analysts believe Hun Sen and his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) fear the king might step down to lead a royalist party to victory at the polls on the back of his grass roots popularity.
